title: Is ‘Summer learning loss’ a thing and what can we do about it?
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton spends a week reading the research on summer learning loss and reports that it exists but is less certain and less dramatic than the online worry suggests. Studies often compare different tests, show losses mainly in maths and some reading skills, and find that most students recover quickly, with inconsistent results by age and background. He ties the cause, as researchers do, to a lack of repeated experiences over the break, and notes that the usual remedies all amount to providing more of them. His own contribution is to argue that coverage-driven schools may overestimate what was ever sticky before the holiday, so some apparent loss is really learning that never took hold. He hypothesises that learning-focused schools suffer less loss, calls for lighter curriculums, and concludes that we should not panic children or parents about it.
points: Research confirms some summer loss, mainly in maths and some reading skills, but the evidence is weaker and more mixed than popular worry assumes.
Researchers mostly attribute loss to an absence of repeated experiences, so all the remedies come down to providing more repeated experiences more consistently.
Apparent loss may partly reflect teaching that was judged learned because it was covered, not because it was ever made sticky.
Skelton hypothesises that schools focused on the quality and quantity of repeated experiences, and on knowing whether learning is happening, lose less over summer.
Overloaded curriculums encourage coverage, so lightening them would help learning be sticky before the break begins.
quotes: Almost all researchers attribute the cause of summer learning loss to an absence of appropriate repeated experiences over the summer break.

Some of the data from research is based on children and students taking different tests. In other words, the results from Test A at the beginning of summer are compared to the results of a different test B on return to school.
Whatever the suggested activities are that might remediate a supposed or actual summer learning loss they all come down to the same thing: provide more repeated experiences more consistently.
Having ‘covered’ something in the curriculum last year as a teacher does not mean that my children or students have learned it or that the ‘coverage’ I provided enabled stickiness to take place.
It might just be that we can reduce apparent post-summer learning loss by making sure that pre-summer learning is truly sticky.

Schools that get learning know that learning loss - at any time - is a natural part of the learning process. If it wasn’t, then we wouldn’t need repeated experiences over time; just one experience would do.
